entries.clue: Refrain from eating, with final twist, such unhealthy foods (4)

indicatorNotes.with final twist: A twist at the end turns only the end round, so the last two letters of the word in front change places.

blocks.note: to fast is to go without food, which is what refraining from eating amounts to

annotation.surface: Somebody giving up food and then adding one last flourish to the diet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Refrain' is the verb here, though in a puzzle this full of music it offers itself as a chorus. Only the last two letters move, which is all a twist at the end asks for.
annotation.definitionFit: Fat is the food component every piece of health advice tells you to cut down on, so the plural names that class of foods.

entries.clue: First in school by a long way, is visibly pleased (6)

blocks.note: the letter standing first in the word school
beating something by a long way is beating it by miles

annotation.surface: A pupil who has come top of the school by a distance and is beaming about it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'First in school' is a position on the surface and a single letter in the parse. The puzzle's jazz names keep surfacing inside ordinary words, and a trumpeter's first name is sitting in this one.
annotation.definitionFit: To smile is to show pleasure on the face, so the third-person verb drops straight into the place 'is visibly pleased' holds.

entries.clue: Duke is thoroughly acquainted with good style (10)

blocks.note: to be well in with somebody is to be thoroughly acquainted with them, on close terms
g is the standard short form for good, as on a school report
ton is fashion or the fashionable world, borrowed from French and kept alive by crosswords

annotation.surface: A nobleman who knows all the best tailors.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Duke' names the man by his title rather than defining him, which is how a dukedom gets to be a definition. A second Duke is hiding here: take the first letter off WELLINGTON and Ellington appears.
annotation.definitionFit: The first Duke of Wellington, the general who beat Napoleon at Waterloo, is known by his dukedom, so 'Duke' names him by example.

entries.clue: Parts of records – they’re not supposed to be heard by other players (6)

annotation.definition2: they’re not supposed to be heard by other players

blocks.note: the featured half of a single, the side the label wanted played

blocks.clueFragment: they’re not supposed to be heard by other players
blocks.note: on stage, lines thrown to the audience that the rest of the cast are deemed not to hear

annotation.surface: Tracks on an album that the rest of the band would rather nobody played.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Players' have instruments on the surface and lines in the parse — actors have been players since Shakespeare. One reading hyphenates and the other does not, a difference the grid quietly swallows.
annotation.definitionFit: A-sides are the featured halves of singles, so 'parts of records' names them; and asides are the remarks an actor speaks past the other characters, unheard by them.

entries.clue: Rely, oddly, on saxophonist as singer (8)

indicatorNotes.oddly: Oddly means strangely here rather than every other letter, and letters treated strangely do not stay in the order they were handed over in.

blocks.note: four letters shuffled into the little harp of the Greeks
Charlie Parker was known as Bird, the most famous nickname in the music

annotation.surface: Leaning on a sax player to carry the vocal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' looks like the instruction to take alternate letters and only means strangely, which is the whole difficulty of the first half. The creature itself is the Australian mimic that can copy a car alarm or a chainsaw.
annotation.definitionFit: The lyrebird's song copies every other bird in the forest note for note, so 'singer' is a plain and fair label for it.

entries.clue: In spelling performance, initially omit ‘c’ in ‘mischief’ (4)

indicatorNotes.initially omit: Initially points at the front of a word, so the letter named is taken from the start and not from anywhere inside.

blocks.note: a spell cast is a charm, so a performance of spelling is one of those
the clue names the letter to be dropped, inside its own quotation marks

annotation.surface: A spelling bee in which the contestant leaves a letter out of a long word.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spelling' is the witchcraft sense, not the schoolroom one the surface sets up. The quotation marks are the setter being helpful for once: they mark a letter and a word to be taken at face value.
annotation.definitionFit: Doing somebody a mischief is the British way of saying you did them harm, so the two nouns cover the same damage.

entries.clue: One introduced to maintain, say, disrupted festivals (8)

indicatorNotes.introduced to: Something introduced to a thing is put inside it, so this letter goes into the middle of the word beside it rather than in front.
indicatorNotes.disrupted: A disrupted thing has been thrown out of its proper order, so those letters are not to be taken as they stand.

blocks.note: to hold a position is to maintain it
the Roman numeral for one
three letters shuffled

annotation.surface: One person brought in to keep order while the celebrations fall apart.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Say' is not the usual 'for example' — it is three letters of fodder, and the comma after it does nothing to help. Billie Holiday is the theme's singer, hiding in a word that began life meaning holy days.
annotation.definitionFit: Holidays are the days kept as feasts and celebrations — Christmas, Easter, a bank holiday — which is what festivals are.

entries.clue: So-called King of jazz, or another one accompanied by string trio (4)

annotation.definition2: another one accompanied by string trio

blocks.note: 'so-called' is the giveaway: the crown was a stage billing, worn by the trio pianist who became a velvet-voiced balladeer

blocks.clueFragment: another one accompanied by string trio
blocks.note: the nursery rhyme's merry old soul called for his pipe, his bowl and his fiddlers three

annotation.surface: Two kings of music, one of them backed by three strings.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves are the same surname: the crooner billed as royalty and the merry old soul of the rhyme, whose fiddlers three are the string trio. This column runs on into 16 down to name a third jazz giant.
annotation.definitionFit: Nat King Cole was billed as a king without being one, and Old King Cole is the rhyme's merry old soul — the same name doing both jobs.

entries.clue: Sly e-mails recycled without end (9)

indicatorNotes.recycled: Recycled material is broken up and made into something else out of the same stuff, which is exactly what happens to these letters.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters, the hyphen counting for nothing
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Scam messages being sent round and round for ever.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Without end' reads as the endless resending the surface describes, and it is the definition: an end is a purpose, as in 'to what end?'. Those two words carry no letters at all.
annotation.definitionFit: To do something aimlessly is to do it with no end in view, 'end' in its older sense of goal or purpose.

entries.clue: Excited by ring to great extent (1,4)

blocks.note: agog is all eager anticipation, ears pricked for the next thing
a ring is a circle, and the letter that draws one

annotation.surface: Somebody thrilled by the telephone going.
annotation.walkthrough: The enumeration gives the shape away: one letter, then four. The phrase is French à gogo, galore, which English picked up from the 1960s discotheques that put it on their signs.
annotation.definitionFit: A gogo means galore or in abundance — champagne a gogo — which is doing or having something to a great extent.

entries.clue: Sign of inexperienced driver, unfortunately reversing into shrub (5)

indicatorNotes.reversing: A car reversing goes back the way it came, so everything assembled in front of this word is read from its far end.

blocks.note: a British learner driver shows a red L-plate front and back
alas is the old word for unfortunately

annotation.surface: A learner backing the car into a bush.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole assembly turns, not just one piece of it, which is why the single letter ends up at the back. Salal is a North American evergreen, grown here mainly for the dark leaves florists pack round bouquets.
annotation.definitionFit: Salal is a low evergreen shrub of the Pacific north-west, leathery-leaved and dark-berried, so it gets the plain word 'shrub'.

entries.clue: Doctor armed with positive response, as in a trance (9)

indicatorNotes.Doctor: To doctor something is to tamper with it, and tampered letters come out in a different order from the one they went in.

blocks.note: five letters shuffled
the approving tap given to a post on social media

annotation.surface: A doctor turning up armed and getting a cheerful yes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' is a verb sitting at the front of the clue, where a solver expects a noun and a definition. The positive response is the social media tap — a sense the word has only carried for twenty years.
annotation.definitionFit: Something dreamlike has the soft, unreal quality of a dream, which is how the world looks to somebody in a trance.

entries.clue: Is breaking up cartel’s revolting behaviour (7)

annotation.definitionNote: Risings are countable acts of revolt, while 'revolting behaviour' is an uncountable phrase; the setter uses it to name the whole of what rebels do rather than to count them.

indicatorNotes.breaking up: To break something up is to split it open, so the word standing in front of this goes into the gap that leaves.

blocks.note: punctuation is never binding, so read past the apostrophe: cartels are price-fixing rings
the clue's own word, taken exactly as it stands

annotation.surface: A cartel's ugly conduct being broken up.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe is there for the surface only — a solver is entitled to ignore any punctuation. 'Revolting' offers itself as the adjective for disgusting, and the definition needs the noun sense of revolt instead.
annotation.definitionFit: A rising is an insurrection — the Easter Rising, the risings of 1745 — so the plural names precisely what people in revolt do.

entries.clue: After removing head, open up fish (5)

indicatorNotes.After removing: What has been removed is gone, so the part named next comes away from the word that follows.

blocks.note: to broach a cask or a subject is to open it up
the head of a word is the letter at its front, and that is the one that goes

annotation.surface: Taking the head off a fish before slitting it open.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Head' points at the first letter of a word that has not been named yet, so the instruction arrives before the thing it acts on. Max Roach, the theme's drummer, shares his name with the fish.
annotation.definitionFit: The roach is a silvery freshwater fish of the carp family, common in British rivers and the staple catch of coarse anglers.

entries.clue: Minimal time, correspondingly reduced for businessperson’s date (7)

indicatorNotes.correspondingly reduced: Correspondence is where words get cut short, so the second sense wants this one in the clipped form a letter-writer would use.

blocks.note: the shortest stretch of time there is, over before you have noticed it
commercial letters date themselves 'the 5th inst.', meaning the fifth of the current month

annotation.surface: A tiny stretch of time, trimmed to fit a company diary.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Correspondingly' is a pun on correspondence: cut the word down for a business letter and you get the inst. that sits beside a date. Both halves define the same word, one in full and one abbreviated.
annotation.definitionFit: An instant is the smallest slice of time there is; and in commercial usage the instant is the current month, which is what the 'inst.' against a date stands for.

entries.clue: Executive supporting firm is major asset (6,4)

indicatorNotes.supporting: A support sits underneath whatever it holds up, so in this column the piece named first ends up at the bottom.

blocks.note: firm in the sense of solid and unyielding, as in a firm grip
office slang for a senior manager, named for what they wear

annotation.surface: A manager propping up the company that employs him.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Firm' looks like the business the executive works for and is the adjective instead. The phrase comes from card games, where your strong suit is the one you hold most of.
annotation.definitionFit: Your strong suit is the thing you are best at and lead with, which is what calling something a major asset says about it.

entries.clue: Form of transport, i.e. coach (5)

blocks.note: the thing that runs on rails, engine and carriages together
the verb: to coach a team is to put it through its paces

annotation.surface: Naming a way of getting about and then explaining what it is.
annotation.walkthrough: 'I.e.' pretends to be an explanation, which invites you to read the last word as a carriage — one part of the thing just named. It is the verb, and this column reads on from 8 down to give a saxophonist.
annotation.definitionFit: A train is the rolling stock that carries passengers along rails, and to train somebody is to coach them, drilling them towards a standard.

entries.clue: Check out books from car ahead of time (5)

indicatorNotes.ahead of: What is ahead of something goes in front of it, so this piece is written before the letter that follows.

blocks.note: the German marque with four rings on the grille
t is the standard short form for time

annotation.surface: Borrowing books out of a car before they are due back.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Check out books' is the whole definition, and the books are accounts rather than the library's stock. The car is a four-letter gift crosswords reach for whenever a make is called for.
annotation.definitionFit: To audit is to go through a set of accounts — the books — and certify them, which is checking the books out in the inspecting sense.

entries.clue: Frenzied divas caught up in international court event (5,3)

indicatorNotes.Frenzied: A frenzy throws everything about, so the letters beside it will not stay in the order they are given.

blocks.note: five letters shuffled
c is how a cricket scorecard records a batter caught out
the clue's own word, taken as it stands

annotation.surface: Temperamental singers swept up in a tennis tournament.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Caught up in' reads as one idiom and is three separate pieces of machinery. The event is the knockout between national men's tennis teams, played every year since 1900, and Miles is why the theme wanted it.
annotation.definitionFit: The Davis Cup is the annual competition between countries' men's tennis teams, so 'international court event' describes it without naming the sport.

entries.clue: New growth in bulb you planted last of all (3)

indicatorNotes.last of all: Last of all asks for the final letter of each of the words named, taken in the order they come.

blocks.note: the closing letter of each of these three words, read left to right

annotation.surface: The first shoot showing from a bulb put in last season.
annotation.walkthrough: The instruction sits at the very end of the clue, where it reads as part of the gardening rather than as an order. Bud Powell is the theme's pianist.
annotation.definitionFit: A bud is the first swelling of new growth on a plant, the stage before it opens into leaf or flower.

entries.clue: Bandleader helps Mingus and others (8)

blocks.note: the leader of a band is the letter standing at its front
to assist is to help, and the third person matches

annotation.surface: The man out front lending a hand to Mingus and the rest of the group.
annotation.walkthrough: Charles Mingus played the double bass and led his own groups, so the definition names a whole class of musician by one member of it. 'Bandleader' is a single word doing the letter-picking, which is easy to read past.
annotation.definitionFit: Charles Mingus was a double-bass player, so naming him and others points at everyone who plays that instrument.

entries.clue: One emperor backing follower of another (5)

indicatorNotes.backing: Something backing is going the other way, so in an across entry these letters are read from right to left.

blocks.note: the indefinite article stands in for one
the tsar was the emperor of all the Russias

annotation.surface: One emperor's supporter standing behind another.
annotation.walkthrough: Both emperors are real. The Russian one supplies the letters; the Ethiopian one, Haile Selassie — Ras Tafari before his coronation — is the other the definition means.
annotation.definitionFit: A Rasta reveres Haile Selassie, emperor of Ethiopia, whose earlier title Ras Tafari gave the movement its name, so the definition points at a second emperor.

entries.clue: Around front area, enjoys capital cigars (7)

indicatorNotes.Around: Around says one piece is wrapped outside the others, so the letters it points past end up in the middle.

blocks.note: to have something is to enjoy it, in the way one enjoys good health
the van is the leading part of an advancing army, as in vanguard
a is the standard short form for area

annotation.surface: Somebody near the front of the crowd enjoying the finest cigars.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Capital' reads as the old-fashioned compliment — a capital fellow, a capital idea — and means the city. The van is the leading part of an army, a sense still alive in 'vanguard'.
annotation.definitionFit: Havanas are cigars rolled from Cuban leaf and named after Havana, Cuba's capital, so the definition identifies them by the city they come from.

entries.clue: Doesn’t go to restaurant having too much noise and drug crime (5,2)

blocks.note: a din is a racket loud enough to complain about
e is ecstasy, the tablet
a sin is an offence against religious law

annotation.surface: A place so loud and so dodgy that somebody stays away from it.
annotation.walkthrough: The three pieces read as one long complaint about the restaurant, and that is what hides the joins. 'Drug' for a single E is worth pocketing: it turns up whenever a clue needs one letter and a whiff of danger.
annotation.definitionFit: To dine in is to eat at home instead of going out, so somebody who dines in is exactly somebody not going to a restaurant.

entries.clue: Piece to play that’s part of falling sequence, in theory (6)

annotation.definition2: part of falling sequence, in theory

blocks.note: the little oblong tile with pips at each end, turned face down at the start of a game

blocks.clueFragment: part of falling sequence, in theory
blocks.note: the Cold War doctrine that one country turning communist would topple the next, named after those tiles stood on end

annotation.surface: A games piece in a chain of collapses, at least on paper.
annotation.walkthrough: Both readings are the same object: the tile you play, and the tile stood on end in a row. 'In theory' is the nudge towards the Cold War doctrine that borrowed the image, and Fats Domino keeps the theme going.
annotation.definitionFit: A domino is the pipped tile you play in the game, and a row of dominoes toppling is the picture behind the domino theory of one fall causing the next.

entries.clue: Name of girl making second statement on first birthday (6)

blocks.note: s is the standard short form for the unit of time
what a child announces on her first birthday is 'I'm one'

annotation.surface: A girl announcing her age at her own party.
annotation.walkthrough: The joke is nearly the whole of the wordplay: a toddler's proudest sentence with a unit of time bolted on the front. Nina Simone is the theme's singer.
annotation.definitionFit: Simone is a French girl's given name, the feminine of Simon, so 'name of girl' defines it by its class rather than by a synonym.

entries.clue: Morbid gratification thus found in endless male posturing (9)

indicatorNotes.found in: What is found in something is inside it, so this piece sits within the word that follows rather than beside it.
indicatorNotes.endless: An endless word has nothing at the end of it any more: the final letter is dropped before anything else happens.

blocks.note: machismo is aggressive male pride, here with its last letter gone
thus and so are the same little word of inference

annotation.surface: Somebody getting a sick thrill out of all that macho swagger.
annotation.walkthrough: The pleasure and the posturing belong to one sentence on the surface, which is what makes the container hard to see. Machismo is Spanish macho, male, taken into English whole in the 1940s.
annotation.definitionFit: Masochism is taking pleasure in one's own pain or humiliation, so 'morbid gratification' names the unhealthy enjoyment at the heart of it.

entries.clue: Order member out of symposium on knowledge (4)

indicatorNotes.out of: Out of names where a thing is taken from, so the letters wanted are sitting inside the words that follow.

blocks.note: four consecutive letters, picking up the end of the first word, the whole of the second and the start of the third

annotation.surface: A man in holy orders walking out of a conference about what we know.
annotation.walkthrough: The run straddles three words, which is why it stays invisible: the eye reads words, not letters. Thelonious Monk is the theme's pianist, and the definition is the monastery sense.
annotation.definitionFit: A monk is a man under vows in a religious order, so 'order member' names him by the institution he has joined.

entries.clue: Baton that may be used for musical performances (4)

annotation.definition2: that may be used for musical performances
annotation.definitionNote: The second definition is a relative clause where a noun would normally stand: it describes a place, reading as '[somewhere] that may be used for musical performances'.

blocks.note: the heavy stick a policeman carries, or the caveman's weapon in a cartoon

blocks.clueFragment: that may be used for musical performances
blocks.note: the small venue with a stage at one end, where the music happens late

annotation.surface: A conductor's baton and the concerts it is waved at.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Baton' invites the conductor's stick, and the answer is the other kind, the one used on people. The venue sense is the theme's home ground: a jazz club is where every one of these players worked.
annotation.definitionFit: A club is a thick stick swung as a weapon, which is what a baton is; and a club is also the late-night room a band gets booked into.

entries.clue: Large number of Romans in unspecified battlefield (5)

indicatorNotes.in: In puts one thing inside another, so the letter named before it goes into the middle of the word that follows.

blocks.note: some is the word for a quantity nobody has pinned down
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

annotation.surface: A vague count of Roman soldiers somewhere on a battlefield.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Large number of Romans' is a numeral rather than a crowd — a thousand of anything, written the Roman way. The river in northern France gave its name to the 1916 battle whose first day is the bloodiest in British army history.
annotation.definitionFit: The Somme is a river in Picardy, and the 1916 battle fought along it took the river's name, so 'battlefield' points at the place through what happened there.

entries.clue: She can be spotted going back and forth in parallel lanes (4)

indicatorNotes.can be spotted: Something that can be spotted is there to be found rather than spelt out, so the letters are sitting inside the words as they stand.
indicatorNotes.going back and forth: Back and forth offers both directions, so the run can be picked up travelling either way through the letters.

blocks.note: four consecutive letters run backwards inside the first word, and four more run forwards across the gap into the second

annotation.surface: A woman spotted pacing up and down between two marked lanes.
annotation.walkthrough: The setter supplies the run twice over, once each way, which is generous and also the joke: two lanes, two directions. Ella Fitzgerald is the theme's singer.
annotation.definitionFit: Ella is a woman's given name — and in Spanish the very word for 'she' — so the bare pronoun is asking for a female name.

entries.clue: A run rearranged, you said, in island country (5)

indicatorNotes.rearranged: Rearranged furniture is the same furniture in different places, and these are the same letters in a different order.

blocks.note: four letters of fodder, taken as the clue writes them
said aloud, the pronoun is a single letter, and it joins the shuffle

annotation.surface: You claimed a single run had been shifted about.
annotation.walkthrough: 'You said' is not an instruction to hear the whole clue aloud; it turns the pronoun itself into the letter you hear when you say it. Nauru is eight square miles of Pacific coral, the smallest republic in the world.
annotation.definitionFit: Nauru is one coral island in the central Pacific and an independent republic, so 'island country' describes the whole of it.

entries.clue: Last one in – that could be stress-related (9)

indicatorNotes.could be: Could be says the letters in front might be read as something else, and letters that might be something else are not fixed in the order given.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Arriving last, which somebody suggests might be down to nerves.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Could be' is a mild anagram indicator, easily read as the speaker hedging rather than as an order. 'Last' looks like an instruction to take a final letter and is simply part of the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Tensional means of or relating to tension, and tension is what stress is in both the engineering sense and the nervous one.
